channel.title: Morperhaus Concert Archives — Liner Notes
channel.description: Weekly stories from 42 years of live music. First-person editorial posts about patterns, discoveries, and moments from a personal concert history spanning 1984 to present.

item.title: Concert #150: My 150th Show
item.description: I didn't plan for my 150th show to land on X at Pacific Amphitheatre, but I couldn't have picked a better bill if I'd tried: The Blasters and Los Lobos opening in Costa Mesa on August 1, 2022. My first show was Adam Ant at Irvine Meadows back in 1984, which puts 38 years between that night and this one. Funny how the number snuck up on me somewhere around the second opener, and I only did the math afterward. Thirty-eight years, 150 shows, and I still got the same jolt when the band walked out.

item.title: Gwen Stefani Walked On for The Brian Setzer Orchestra
item.description: Swing revival acts didn't usually share stages with ska-punk singers, which is what made August 8, 1998 at the Greek Theatre stand out in my notebook: Gwen Stefani walked on with The Brian Setzer Orchestra for "You're the Boss." I'd only seen her once before, with No Doubt, a full ten years earlier at Disneyland back in 1988. One show, one decade apart, one unexpected duet — that's the whole file I have on Gwen Stefani, and I wouldn't trade it for a longer one.

item.title: Thompson Twins in 1984: What Was in the Air
item.description: Four shows on my calendar in 1984, and one of them was Thompson Twins at Irvine Meadows on May 12, part of an amphitheater that had only opened three years earlier, in 1981. I keep coming back to how much of new wave that year got built on the strength of MTV, which by 1984 had turned bands like the Thompson Twins into faces as much as sounds, and standing on that lawn in Irvine put me right in the middle of it. Four shows that whole year, and I chose to spend one of them on a band whose entire aesthetic depended on a channel that was barely three years old. I didn't think about any of that in the moment, I just remember the synths carrying across an amphitheater still new enough to smell like fresh concrete.

item.title: Ziggy Marley — 17.4 Years Before Love Is My Religion
item.description: There's something almost funny about catching a reggae artist 14.6 years before his first solo album, but that's what happened when I saw Ziggy Marley at Mesa Amphitheatre in 1988. Love Is My Religion wouldn't arrive until 2006, nearly 209 months after that Arizona night, and seven more albums would follow it that I also couldn't have imagined. Two of the five songs I still reach for from that record trace back to a show where none of it existed yet. I like sitting with that gap — proof that the artist I watched in 1988 was still becoming someone, and I just happened to be in the room years before he knew who that was either.

item.title: Garbage — 17 Songs From The Album That Shares Their Name, Live
item.description: I have seen Garbage perform 17 different songs tied to their debut album across 6 shows, stretching from 2005 all the way to 2022, and I still find that number a little staggering. That self-titled record never left the setlists I caught — "Only Happy When It Rains" and "Stupid Girl" turned up at all six shows and "Vow" at five, like they knew those songs were worth defending. The 9:30 Club show in October 2015 sits at the center of that run for me, right around the time of the album's 20th anniversary remaster, and there was something almost defiant about hearing those songs played that loud in that room. Some bands make peace with their past; Garbage just keeps performing it like it's still an argument they intend to win.

item.title: 3 Concerts in 12 Days
item.description: I don't know what got into me in July 2023, but I saw 3 shows across 3 different genres in 12 days without once feeling like I was overdoing it. Foals at The Belasco on the 18th, UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st, X at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on the 30th — indie rock, reggae, and punk, all inside a single Southern California summer. There's something about that stretch that still makes me smile: I went from the close, sweaty energy of The Belasco to an amphitheatre in Orange County without stopping to ask whether any of it made sense as a playlist. It didn't, and that was exactly the point.

item.title: Social Distortion — 1.4 Years Before Born to Kill
item.description: Punk rock has always been about the song before the studio catches up, and at The Belasco in Los Angeles on December 6, 2024, I heard four tracks from Born to Kill a full 518 days before the record existed in anyone's hands. Four songs — "Tonight," "Over You," "The Way Things Were," and the title track itself — dropped into an 18-song set like they'd always belonged there, which, knowing Social Distortion, they probably had for years already. That's the thing about a band formed in 1978: they don't audition new material, they road-test it, and the crowd at The Belasco had no idea they were the test.

item.title: "Notorious": Nile Rodgers and Duran Duran, 39 Years Apart
item.description: "Notorious" is a song with two owners in a sense: Duran Duran wrote it, and Nile Rodgers produced it. I heard Duran Duran play it at Irvine Meadows in July 1987, and then 39 years later I watched Rodgers claim it fully at the Pacific Amphitheatre, playing it as his own with complete justification. Two different Southern California venues, two different summers, the same song landing with the same authority both times.

item.title: July 31: 40 Years Since The Art of Noise
item.description: I drove down to the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 31, 1986, genuinely unsure what a live Art of Noise show would even look like — they were a studio project, built from samples and synthesizers, and the stage setup felt more like a science experiment than a concert. It's been 40 years since that night, and I still remember the disorientation of watching music that seemed to exist only on record suddenly fill an outdoor amphitheatre with actual air and heat and crowd noise. They had already released (Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise? by then, and hearing those fractured rhythms in the open California summer felt genuinely strange in the best way. Some shows you attend; that one attended me.

item.title: Pacific Amphitheatre: 17 Shows Over 5 Decades
item.description: I keep coming back to Pacific Amphitheatre, seventeen times now, and the span still gets me: Tears For Fears on July 10, 1985, and Nile Rodgers on July 31, 2026. That's five decades under the same Costa Mesa sky, from the Songs from the Big Chair era straight through to a stage I still can't quite believe I was standing in front of in July 2026. In between, Run-DMC, UB40, the Art of Noise, the Beach Boys — fifteen artists total, and somehow this one amphitheater kept pulling me back for all of them. I don't have a tidy reason why. I just know I never once regretted the drive.

item.title: July 16: 40 Years Since Beach Boys
item.description: I was at the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 16, 1986 — 40 years ago today — and I still remember the way the summer air felt when the opening notes hit. The Beach Boys had been together 25 years by then, and somehow they made those harmonies sound like they were being invented right there in front of me. It was the 15th show in my archive, a little over two years after the first. Forty years later, that night still feels like part of the foundation.

item.title: House of Blues Anaheim: 6 Shows Over 3 Decades
item.description: I still think about walking into House of Blues Anaheim for the first time in August 2003 to see Joe Jackson — an artist who'd been making records since before I probably knew what a record was. Six shows across three decades under that name, from that night with Joe Jackson all the way to Social Distortion in December 2022, with Streetlight Manifesto, Future Islands, and Royal Blood filling the years in between. Five artists who share almost nothing sonically, which tells me the venue was doing something right. Somehow a club in Anaheim became a quiet constant in my concert life, and I never quite planned it that way.

item.title: June 21: 35 Years Since Jimmy Buffett
item.description: I was at Irvine Meadows on June 21, 1991 — 35 years ago today — and I remember the sun going down over the amphitheater in a way that felt almost staged, like the sky was in on the joke. Jimmy Buffett had been playing that Southern California crowd like a warm ocean current, and somewhere between opening with "Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes" and closing with "Margaritaville," the whole place stopped being a concert and started being a backyard party full of strangers. I didn't own a single piece of Parrothead gear, but I understood it completely by the end of the night. Some shows teach you why a fanbase exists — this was one of them.

item.title: No Doubt: Caught Once, Never Again
item.description: Here's something that stopped me cold in my own archive: I saw No Doubt at Disneyland in March 1988 — just two years after they formed — on a bill with The Nylons in Anaheim, before virtually anyone outside Southern California knew their name. That's the only No Doubt entry in my entire archive, which means I caught them exactly once, at what had to be one of their earliest public performances, and never crossed paths with them again through Tragic Kingdom, Rock Steady, or any of the singles years. The fact that my sole sighting happened at a theme park in 1988 is the kind of detail I couldn't have invented.

item.title: Run DMC: Caught Once, Never Again
item.description: I caught Run DMC exactly once in my entire concert history — June 20, 1987 at Pacific Amphitheatre with the Beastie Boys opening. This was right in their Raising Hell era, when both acts were ascending rapidly, and somehow I never managed to see either of them again despite decades of concertgoing. Looking back, that single show captured lightning in a bottle: two pioneering hip-hop acts sharing a stage just as the genre was breaking into the mainstream. I can't believe I never got another Run DMC sighting after that night.

item.title: Sting — Days After Nevermind Dropped
item.description: Nevermind hit shelves on September 24th, 1991, and within days the entire rock landscape had shifted — yet there I was on October 4th, just 10 days later, watching Sting perform his polished pop-rock at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa. I remember thinking how surreal it felt to be watching Sting, with The Soul Cages still his newest album, while the radio was still figuring out what to do with "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The timing captures this perfect moment when the old guard was still touring their greatest hits, completely unaware that the ground had already moved beneath them.

item.title: Blancmange at Crawford Hall: 40 Years On
item.description: I saw Blancmange at Crawford Hall in Irvine on February 15, 1986, and I can still picture Neil Arthur's theatrical gestures up on that stage. They already had three albums out, the newest, Believe You Me, from 1985, and their blend of electronic beats and Arthur's distinctive vocals still felt like the future of pop music. Crawford Hall was an intimate venue for a band that was getting significant radio play, making it feel like catching lightning in a bottle. Looking back, that Saturday in February 1986 captured a specific moment when British new wave was reshaping American college radio.

item.title: April 12: 40 Years Since The Alarm
item.description: I remember standing in that UCLA crowd 40 years ago today, watching The Alarm tear through their set with an intensity that felt almost desperate. Mike Peters had this way of leaning into the microphone like he was trying to pull every person in the venue into whatever urgent message he was delivering, and I was completely susceptible to that kind of raw conviction. Strength was their newest record, and you could feel the band's belief that rock music could still change the world—a notion that seemed both naive and absolutely necessary in 1986. Forty years later, I still get that same surge of adrenaline when "68 Guns" comes on shuffle.

item.title: The Brian Setzer Orchestra: 22 Years of Shows
item.description: I remember discovering The Brian Setzer Orchestra at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach back in 1995, when swing revival was just starting to bubble up from the underground. That first show hooked me on Brian's rockabilly-meets-big-band sound, and I ended up catching them 4 times across 22 years, from that intimate club gig all the way to the Warner Theatre in DC in 2017. Four different venues, three different decades, but always that same electric energy when Brian strapped on his hollow-body Gretsch and the 17-piece orchestra kicked into high gear. There's something deeply satisfying about following an artist long enough to watch both of you age into the music.

item.title: March 22: 13 Years Since Bad Religion
item.description: I remember walking into the 9:30 Club that March night in 2013, thirteen years ago now, and feeling like I was stepping into punk rock church. Bad Religion delivered their signature blend of melody and fury to a packed room, with Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club warming up the crowd beforehand. The whole evening felt like a masterclass in how punk has evolved since Bad Religion formed back in 1980, yet Greg Graffin's voice cut through the years like nothing had changed. Sometimes the best shows are the ones that remind you why you fell in love with live music in the first place.
